title: Morgan DeBaun's Indie Media Post Sparks Pay Debate
htmlContent:
Morgan DeBaun has spent more than a decade as one of the most visible figures in Black digital media. As the founder and CEO of Blavity, she built a company that became a destination for Black readers, writers and creators. So when she took to Instagramto talk about the future of independently owned digital publications, she likely expected a conversation about the challenges facing the industry.

Instead, the comment section became a debate about Blavity itself, touching on layoffs, writer pay and whether Black media companies are truly working together.

A Conversation About Survival

DeBaun's reel focused on the uncertain road ahead for indie-owned digital outlets. Independent publishers have faced shrinking ad budgets, changing search and social algorithms, and the growing influence of artificial intelligence on how audiences find news. For Black-owned media in particular, the pressures have raised questions about who gets access to advertisers and platforms, and who gets left out.

That message struck a nerve, but not entirely in the way DeBaun may have intended.

Writer Tiffany Hamilton Pushes Back

Writer Tiffany Hamilton, who posts as @tffhthewriter, was among the first to challenge DeBaun. She questioned whether Blavity had carried out a major round of layoffs in order to invest in AI, and she raised concerns about what she described as a history of underpaying writers. In her view, those issues needed to be addressed before any conversation about indie outlets being shut out.

Another commenter echoed her concerns, saying she knew two former writers for the company who had complained about low pay and disrespectful treatment. That commenter went as far as saying DeBaun should delete the post.

DeBaun Responds: 'We Sunsetted Our Brands'

DeBaun didn't stay silent. Replying directly to Hamilton, she denied that Blavity's cuts were made to fund AI.

"We didn't do a layoff to invest in ai," she wrote.

She explained that the company shut down some of its brands because readership had fallen to a couple hundred thousand people and advertisers had stopped spending to reach that audience. DeBaun also pushed back on the idea that AI was the motive, pointing to brands such as Home & Texture and 21Ninety and asking why the company would have invested in AI with that business spend.

Questions About Timing and Pay Remain

Hamilton acknowledged the explanation but wasn't fully satisfied. She suggested Blavity may have moved too early, noting that its cuts came months before wider layoffs swept through other media companies.

She then returned to the issue of compensation. Hamilton said that Blavity was once the brand many Black writers dreamed of working for, but that numerous writers, contributors and collaborators shared the same frustration: being paid well below industry standards and then dismissed after raising the issue. She asked DeBaun to address those concerns directly.

Hamilton also brought up a past meeting with DeBaun about a potential video partnership between Blavity and BlackTree TV. She argued that companies like Blavity too often passed on such proposals and chose to build content in-house instead of banding together with other Black-owned outlets.

DeBaun's replies in the thread did not directly respond to the pay allegations.

BlackTree TV Enters the Chat

The exchange took another turn when BlackTree TV, the long-running Black digital video brand, joined the conversation. After a commenter tagged the company, DeBaun responded that Blavity simply couldn't afford to buy every Black media company. She added that Blavity has formed partnerships and joint ventures with more than 20 Black media businesses, naming Baller Alert, Hollywood Unlocked and The Gathering Spot among them.

BlackTree TV fired back.

"We were never for sale, tf?" the account wrote. The company argued that none of those partnerships could have given Blavity access to BlackTree TV's content library, which it says has topped a billion views on YouTube. It also said its traffic is currently up, suggesting that DeBaun should take a closer look at what BlackTree is doing differently.

A Bigger Industry Debate

The back-and-forth highlights tensions that go well beyond one Instagram post. Black-owned media outlets are competing for the same limited pool of advertising dollars while trying to survive industry-wide disruption. At the same time, the writers and creators who power those outlets are increasingly vocal about fair pay and respectful treatment.

DeBaun's point about the economics of digital media is a real one. Brands that lose readers and advertisers often can't survive, no matter who owns them. But her critics raised a fair counterpoint: calls for unity and support ring hollow for some if the people doing the work feel undervalued.

What Comes Next

The conversation DeBaun started is one the industry needs to have. Independent Black media faces serious challenges, and collaboration could be part of the solution. But as her comment section showed, any honest discussion about the future of indie publications will also have to include the writers, partners and competitors who feel they have been left behind along the way.
excerpt: Blavity founder and CEO Morgan DeBaun took to Instagram to discuss the challenges facing independently owned digital outlets, but her comment section quickly turned into a debate about layoffs, writer pay, and whether Black media companies are truly working together.
